prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked GLP-1 first, but unanimity of opening ranks is not itself evidence, so I re-tested the case on its own terms. It is a full arc from hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide in humans, receptor biology) to drugs with replicated outcome benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is stable and independently confirmed, and the clinical scale is current. A prize for the physiology of the peptide, with the discovery-side contributors Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, fits the Physiology or Medicine remit well.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested. The three-person cap forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue design is what made the drugs, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed (and Habener, not on the credited list, has a claim). Rewarding only the discovery side risks a citation that is detached from the therapies the public associates with the prize. Choosing the drug developer over a discoverer, however, would turn it into a pharmaceutical development prize. Neither option is clean.

responses.point: Proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, so that discovery, physiology and therapy are all covered, and noted that Mojsov's allocation cannot be resolved from the supplied text.
responses.response: I take the argument for covering the arc seriously, but I disagree with swapping Mojsov for Knudsen. The prize category is about discovery, and the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is the step that made the physiology actionable. Knudsen's design of long-acting analogues is excellent engineering built on that knowledge, and the Nobel tradition has mostly rewarded the discovery rather than the optimisation. If priority around Mojsov turns out to be unsupportable, I would reopen the question, but I would not start from Knudsen.

responses.point: Ranked TNF blockade (B036, Feldmann and Maini) second as a clean two-person translational milestone for chronic inflammatory disease, mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that anti-TNF therapy is clinically major and has a cleaner attribution than optogenetics or GLP-1. My reservation is conceptual. It is mostly a therapeutic proof of concept built on previously known cytokine biology, and it overlaps with IL-6 blockade, so it is a weaker discovery claim than GLP-1, where basic physiology and clinical effect are both substantial. I would keep it as a credible future prize, not as a competitor for this year, but I would like her to say what she thinks the discovery contribution was beyond the clinical trials.

responses.point: Placed GLP-1 first but flagged that Habener, not on the credited list, may have a claim, and asked whether we should reward the physiology or the drug development.
responses.response: I share the Habener concern and cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence, which is exactly why I would pin the citation to the physiology and the active peptide form instead of naming a single originator. On his second question I would reward the physiology, and I think the committee should be explicit that the citation does not extend to drug design. That keeps the prize defensible even if the historical record on the peptide is argued over afterward.

responses.point: Ranked the unfolded protein response (B014, Mori and Walter) second as a conceptually clean two-person discovery of organelle-to-nucleus signalling.
responses.response: I agree B014 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and a mature, foundational result, which is why I name it as an alternative. My hesitation is that its clinical payoff is still mostly conceptual, with no approved therapy, whereas GLP-1 combines the same level of mechanism with proven patient benefit. I would not argue strongly against B014 as the prize if GLP-1 stalled over the allocation problem.

responses.point: Ranked antisense correction of SMN2 splicing (B001, Krainer and Bennett) second as a clear bridge from RNA biology to the first effective spinal muscular atrophy therapy.
responses.response: The SMA story is compelling and has an attribution that is close to clean, and as a neuroscientist I recognise how much it changed a fatal infantile disease. I qualify it only on scale: the antisense approach so far applies to a small number of diseases, other SMA therapies now compete, and the SMN gene identification (outside the credited names) is part of the story. I regard it as a strong candidate for a later year, and I would not displace GLP-1 with it now.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide can be recognised without Habener, who is not on the credited list.
Whether a three-person cap that excludes Knudsen yields a citation the committee can defend as a physiology prize.
Optogenetics (B028) remains attractive, but the allocation among six names is unresolved, so I leave it outside my configuration.
My recollection of the discovery chronology is from memory and has not been independently checked.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I use optogenetic tools in circuit work as a field user, which is not a personal tie to B028 candidates, and I have no documented connection to the candidates in B027. My documented links (Grillner, Ernfors, Perlmann) do not involve any shortlisted candidate.
